item.text: I found several omitted matches in distinct scenes: Moses’ deposited law, Jeremiah’s witnessed deed, rabbinic readings of Jacob’s final exchange, and additional inheritance and exhortation texts. I’ll save only those new proposals from memory.

item.command:
/bin/bash -lc "cat > enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec10/luna/followup.tsv <<'EOF'
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.26	law deposited beside ark as witness	Moses tells Israel to place the written law beside the ark as a witness; this unites the commentary's inherited instruction, entrusted object, and witness in one testament-like act.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.32.10	witnessed property deed	Jeremiah signs, seals, and has witnesses attest a purchase deed; the legal transfer gives the commentary's rights of heirs and witness scene a concrete documentary analogue.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.32.14	deed preserved for the future	The deed is placed in an earthen vessel so it may last many days; this closely matches the commentary's entrusted legacy preserved for successors.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ruth.4.9	witnesses to a property transfer	Boaz calls the elders and people as witnesses that he has acquired Elimelech's property; this joins property succession to public testimony as the commentary does.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.49.28	father's blessing distributed among heirs	Jacob blesses each of his twelve sons according to his blessing; this is a distinct patriarchal testament in which the father's last words are distributed among successors.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.48.22	extra portion to an heir	Jacob grants Joseph one portion more than his brothers; this concretely develops the commentary's claim that an inheritance consists of apportioned shares.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.13.22	inheritance to grandchildren	The good person leaves an inheritance to children's children; this states directly the intergenerational transfer that the commentary uses to illuminate mutual counsel as a legacy.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.71.18	old age and testimony to generations	The aging speaker asks to remain until he has told the coming generation of God's strength; this gives the commentary's deathbed image a living elder's explicit concern to pass testimony onward.
strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.102.18	writing for a future generation	The psalm says its words are written for a generation yet to come; this makes the commentary's spoken bequest into a preserved written testimony for later believers.
strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Babylonian Talmud, Pesahim 56a	Jacob asks his sons about their faith	The Talmud reads Jacob's deathbed gathering as his asking whether his sons remain faithful, to which they affirm Israel's God; this is a close Jewish interpretation of the commentary's Jacob asking what his sons will worship after him.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.12.13	dispute over inheritance	A man asks Jesus to tell his brother to divide the inheritance with him; this directly stages the claim over heirs' shares that the commentary treats as rights.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.12.14	refusal to arbitrate inheritance	Jesus refuses the role of judge or divider in the inheritance dispute and warns against greed; this contrasts a legal allocation of heirs' rights with a warning that the claim itself can be spiritually misdirected.
strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Luke.12.20	death interrupts accumulation	In the rich fool parable, God asks who will receive the goods the man prepared after his death; this counters confidence in a self-managed estate with the uncertainty of who inherits it.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.1.14	guarantee of inheritance	The Spirit is called the pledge of the believers' inheritance until its redemption; this closely joins the commentary's guarantor standing behind a claim with heirs awaiting their due.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.11.23	received and handed on	Paul says he handed on what he first received about the Lord's Supper; this is a Christian formula for preserving a teaching and ritual across generations, matching the commentary's word passed from one believer to another.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.11.25	covenant remembered in a rite	The cup is identified with the new covenant and the rite is to be repeated in remembrance; this gives the commentary's transmitted counsel a specific liturgical form of communal remembrance.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.3.14	continuing in received teaching	Timothy is told to continue in what he learned and believed, knowing from whom he learned it; this explicitly links faith to a trustworthy chain of teachers, as the commentary links faith to counsel passed onward.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:2Tim.4.2	exhortation with patience	In the final charge before the writer speaks of his approaching death, Timothy is told to correct, rebuke, and exhort with complete patience and teaching; this directly pairs the commentary's mutual counsel with ṣabr.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.11	mutual encouragement	The community is told to encourage one another and build one another up; this is a direct formulaic counterpart to the commentary's reciprocal act of enjoining one another.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.24	stirring one another to good works	The readers are to consider how to provoke one another to love and good works; this directly joins reciprocal exhortation to the commentary's faithful people's good action.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.10.25	communal encouragement	The readers are told to keep assembling and encourage one another; this makes mutual counsel an ongoing communal practice rather than a solitary last instruction.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.6.17	oath securing heirs' promise	God confirms the promise to its heirs with an oath; this directly combines the commentary's heirs and sworn testimony, showing an oath used to assure rather than test a claimant.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.21.38	attempt to seize the heir's inheritance	The tenants identify the owner's son as heir and kill him in hopes of taking his inheritance; this counter-scene makes the commentary's concern with heirs' rights vivid through their violent denial.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Thess.5.11	one another built up	Paul's instruction does not merely pass advice from a dying teacher; it requires believers to build each other up, adding a reciprocal community structure to the commentary's inheritance metaphor.
medium	tevrat	paralel	WLC:Deut.31.7	Moses charges Joshua before Israel	Moses publicly tells Joshua to be strong and lead the people into the land; this is a succession charge from a departing leader to the person who will carry the community forward.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.31.24	law written before Moses' death	Moses completes writing the law in a book before the farewell scene ends; together with its deposit by the ark, this makes the instruction a durable object for later generations.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.48.5	grandsons adopted as heirs	Jacob declares Joseph's two sons to be his own sons for inheritance; this extends the commentary's discussion of who receives a share beyond the obvious line of sons.
medium	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Gen.48.19	younger son favored over elder	Jacob predicts that the younger Ephraim will become greater than Manasseh, reversing birth order in a blessing; this complicates any reading of inherited portions as an unalterable firstborn entitlement.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ruth.4.10	name preserved through succession	Boaz explains that redeeming the property also preserves the dead man's name; this adds the continuation of a deceased person's household identity to the commentary's material inheritance and testament.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Jer.32.15	land to be possessed again	Jeremiah's witnessed deed is interpreted by the promise that houses, fields, and vineyards will again be bought in the land; this frames the preserved document as a promise to future inheritors.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Ps.2.7	Arabic ḥ-q-q / Hebrew ḥ-q-q; package table's sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary labels بِٱلْحَقّ with Arabic root ḥ-q-q and describes a binding right; the Hebrew king announces a חֹק, a decree, from the candidate root חקק, so the psalm shows a related legal sense without proving cognacy.
medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.2.8	son receives an inheritance	The royal son is promised the nations as his inheritance; this develops the commentary's image of a binding grant passing from a father to an heir.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.32.4	Arabic ʾ-m-n / Hebrew ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary labels ءَامَنُوا۟ with Arabic root ʾ-m-n; Deuteronomy joins Hebrew אֱמוּנָה, faithfulness, with God's justice and uprightness, bringing the commentary's adjacent faith and al-ḥaqq together while leaving the sound-based cognacy unverified.
medium	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Dan.6.4	Arabic ʾ-m-n / Aramaic ʾ-m-n; package table's sound correspondence, unverified	The commentary labels faith with Arabic root ʾ-m-n; Aramaic describes Daniel as מְהֵימַן, faithful, in a court where officials can find no fault except by attacking his observance of God's law, joining the root candidate to testimony and legal pressure.
medium	tevrat	motif	Mishnah, Shevuot 4:1	oath of testimony	The Mishnah defines the legal scope of an oath of testimony and the witnesses bound by it; it adds a rabbinic procedure for the compulsory witness oath that the commentary develops.
medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Genesis Rabbah 98:2	Jacob's interrupted disclosure	A midrash on Jacob gathering his sons reads the scene as his attempt to reveal the end of days, interrupted when the Divine Presence departs; this shifts the deathbed words from a family bequest toward an eschatological disclosure. Section numbering can vary by edition.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.1.13	sealed after believing	Believers are sealed with the promised Spirit after hearing and believing the message; this adds a seal of authentication to the commentary's pairing of entrusted faith and a guarantor.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.8.17	heirs through suffering	Paul calls believers heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ, provided they suffer with him; this links inheritance with endurance, a combination central to the commentary's reading of faith and ṣabr.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.5.5	meek inherit the land	Jesus promises the land to the meek; this gives the commentary's patience and inheritance motifs an explicit Christian pairing, though in an eschatological rather than legal estate setting.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.13.34	farewell command to love one another	Jesus gives his disciples a command to love one another on the eve of his death; this is a concrete last instruction entrusted to a community, though its content differs from the commentary's truth and patience.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.14.27	peace left with disciples	Jesus says he leaves and gives his peace to the disciples; the farewell gift formula gives a distinct Christian example of a legacy passed to survivors.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.11.25	covenant and remembrance	In Paul's received-and-delivered account of the Supper, the cup is the new covenant and is repeated in remembrance; this links a communal rite to a founder's words preserved after death.
medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Clem.44.1	successors after the apostles' deaths	Clement says the apostles appointed approved successors so that others could succeed them after their deaths; this early Christian account makes the commentary's chain of counsel an explicit succession of entrusted responsibility.
weak	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Gen.20.18	Arabic ʿ-ṣ-r / Hebrew ʿ-ṣ-r; package table's sound correspondence, unverified	The Qur'anic word al-ʿaṣr is an oath by time, but the commentary separately reports a source-lexicon gloss under Arabic root ʿ-ṣ-r of giving and then withdrawing a gift; Genesis uses the Hebrew candidate root עָצַר for God closing wombs, a related withholding sense, not the verse's time oath. The sound correspondence is unverified.
EOF"

item.text:
Saved the new proposals to [followup.tsv](/Volumes/aro/projects/prose_generation/enrichment/bible/work/s103/discovery/s103-20261009/sec10/luna/followup.tsv).

Accuracy concerns: the cited Hebrew/Aramaic root correspondences are unverified sound candidates, and Genesis Rabbah section numbering can vary by edition.
